title: The Insanity of Preparing Students for Jobs That Dont Exist Yet by Using Unproven Methods and Ignoring Fundamentals nproven-methods-and-ignoring-fundamentals
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Rather than developing an original argument, Stuart uses this piece as a recommender’s platform, directing readers to Blake Harvard’s article on the logical absurdities embedded in the ‘preparing students for jobs that don’t exist yet’ rationale for educational reform. He introduces Harvard as a like-minded practicing teacher-writer and shares two extended excerpts that together make the core case: abandoning foundational literacy and numeracy skills in favor of unknowable future-work competencies is circular reasoning, and creativity—the very skill futurist frameworks prize—depends on stored knowledge that students can only develop through structured learning. Stuart lends his platform credibility to Harvard’s more concentrated argument, noting that Harvard accomplishes in a short piece what Stuart could not improve upon.
points: The ‘preparing students for jobs that don’t exist yet’ rationale contains a self-defeating logical contradiction: if we don’t know what those jobs are, we cannot know whether our current methods do or do not prepare students for them.

World Economic Forum projections that reading, writing, and mathematics will be ‘out of focus’ by 2030 undermine their own framework’s goals: creativity, the skill predicted to rise in demand, cannot exist without the knowledge base that foundational literacy and numeracy develop.

Harvard’s formulation ‘You cannot be creative with information you don’t have’ distills the core argument that knowledge and creative skill are not alternatives but dependencies—you need the former to exercise the latter.

Stuart’s curatorial move here models a practice he recommends to teachers: recognize when someone else makes a point better than you can, and direct your audience to that source rather than restating it less effectively.
quotes: Strangely enough, it sometimes feels like what is lost in many supposed leaps forward in education is the basics of learning. From a cognitive perspective, we’re being pushed away from what works in order to prepare students for ‘work that doesn’t exist yet.

If we don’t know of the work our students will be doing when they are out in the workforce, then how can we predict that we’re not preparing them for that unknown world? And how do we know what we should do to prepare them?

reading, writing, and mathematics are predicted to be ‘out of focus’ in 2030; they are less essential now and not expected to increase in use. Wait…what? How it the world will the ability to read and write and perform mathematical computations be less essential?
You cannot be creative with information you don’t have. There’s got to be some understanding and memory of a topic in order to successfully create from that subject.
it’s not a long article (love it), but it’s packed with wisdom. That’s basically the goal here in DSJ Land, but I can’t make the points Blake makes any better than he does.
